These exercises practise the ideas from Chapter 2: vectors, factors, data frames, matrices, and lists. Edit the code in any box and press **Run Code**. Where you see `______`, replace it with your own code.

## Vectors and factors

### Exercise 1: Picking values with a condition

Here are the ages of five students. Show only the ages over 30, then count how many there are.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex1
ages <- c(24, 31, 28, 45, 26)
ages[______]
sum(______)
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex1" }
::: { .callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

The condition is `ages > 30`. Put it inside the brackets to select, and inside `sum()` to count.
:::
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex1" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
ages <- c(24, 31, 28, 45, 26)
ages[ages > 30]
sum(ages > 30)
```

Two students are over 30: those aged 31 and 45.
:::
:::

### Exercise 2: A whole vector at once

Elaf's sleep over five nights is stored below. Convert it to minutes, and find the share of nights shorter than 7 hours.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2
sleep <- c(6.5, 7, 5.5, 8, 6)
sleep * ______
mean(sleep ______ 7)
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex2" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
sleep <- c(6.5, 7, 5.5, 8, 6)
sleep * 60
mean(sleep < 7)
```

`mean()` of a `TRUE`/`FALSE` vector is the share of `TRUE` values: 0.6, or 60% of nights.
:::
:::

### Exercise 3: Ordered categories

Make a factor from these answers whose levels run from `"Disagree"` through `"Neutral"` to `"Agree"`, and check the order with `table()`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3
answers <- factor(c("Agree", "Disagree", "Neutral", "Agree"),
                  levels = ______)
table(answers)
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex3" }
::: { .callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

`levels` takes a vector of the categories in the order you want: `c("Disagree", ______, ______)`.
:::
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex3" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
answers <- factor(c("Agree", "Disagree", "Neutral", "Agree"),
                  levels = c("Disagree", "Neutral", "Agree"))
table(answers)
```
:::
:::

## Elaf's data

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [ex4, ex5, ex6]
students <- read.csv("students.csv")
```

### Exercise 4: Selecting rows

How many students study part-time **and** have children? Fill in the second condition.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4
both <- students[students$study_mode == "Part-time" & ______, ]
nrow(both)
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex4" }
::: { .callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

The variable is `has_children`, and its values are `"Yes"` and `"No"`. Remember `==` for "is equal to".
:::
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex4" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
both <- students[students$study_mode == "Part-time" & students$has_children == "Yes", ]
nrow(both)
```
:::
:::

### Exercise 5: Adding a column

Add a column called `over_30` that is `TRUE` for students older than 30, then count them. Run it first as it is: why is the answer `NA`?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5
students$over_30 <- students$age > 30
sum(students$over_30)
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex5" }
::: { .callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

One student's age is missing, so one value of `over_30` is `NA`. `sum()` has an `na.rm` argument, just like `mean()`.
:::
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex5" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
students$over_30 <- students$age > 30
sum(students$over_30, na.rm = TRUE)
table(students$over_30)   # table() leaves NA out unless you ask for it
```
:::
:::

### Exercise 6: Categories as a factor

Turn `faculty` into a factor and list its levels. How many levels are there?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6
students$faculty <- ______(students$faculty)
levels(students$faculty)
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex6" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
students$faculty <- factor(students$faculty)
levels(students$faculty)
length(levels(students$faculty))   # 5 faculties
```
:::
:::

## Matrices and lists

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [ex7, ex8]
semesters <- read.csv("semesters.csv")
```

### Exercise 7: A correlation matrix

Calculate the correlations between GPA, sleep, and wellbeing, round them to two decimal places, and pick out the correlation between sleep and wellbeing.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex7
vars <- semesters[, c("gpa", "sleep_hours", "wellbeing")]
correlations <- cor(vars, use = "complete.obs")
round(correlations, 2)
correlations["______", "______"]
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex7" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
vars <- semesters[, c("gpa", "sleep_hours", "wellbeing")]
correlations <- cor(vars, use = "complete.obs")
round(correlations, 2)
correlations["sleep_hours", "wellbeing"]
```
:::
:::

### Exercise 8: Results are lists

Run a t-test asking whether students sleep 7 hours on average in their first semester. The result is a list: list its parts with `names()`, then pick out the p-value.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex8
first_semester <- semesters[semesters$semester == 1, ]
result <- t.test(first_semester$sleep_hours, mu = 7)
names(result)
result$______
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex8" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
first_semester <- semesters[semesters$semester == 1, ]
result <- t.test(first_semester$sleep_hours, mu = 7)
names(result)
result$p.value
```

The p-value is tiny: students sleep clearly less than 7 hours on average. Chapter 6 explains what a p-value means.
:::
:::
